## 1. What was read

**736 research articles** from 32 of the 33 journals on the roster.

A further **212** records (22% of the 948 this month's harvest returned) carry no abstract and are not research: news, correspondence, editor highlights and obituaries. PubMed types them `Journal Article` and nothing else, so the publication-type filter cannot see them — across the whole index they are 22.7% of it and 35% of `general`, and 3,801 of them are JAMA. Every count below is over the full harvest and is inflated by this; the figure above is not.

| General | Cancer | Immune | Bioinfo | Sysbio |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 484 | 139 | 77 | 226 | 22 |

!!! warning "Volume swing against the median month: cancer -25%"
    Check the source before reading anything into this. Two benign causes account for most of these. `bioinfo` every January carries the Nucleic Acids Research database issue and runs high. And several journals simply deposit nothing in some months: across the 44 months read, 4 of 33 journals are absent from at least one, worst being *Nat Mach Intell* (20 months missing, 81 papers in total) and *Bioinformatics* (4 months missing, 2,905 papers in total). This month is missing *Nat Mach Intell*. Queried directly, PubMed returns zero for those journal-months too — the holes are in the source, reproduced exactly by re-running the harvest. So a swing here is not evidence that a field went quiet, and is not usually evidence that the pipeline broke either.

Largest contributors: Nature 114, Science 89, JAMA 82, Nucleic Acids Res 77, Bioinformatics 60, Cell 49.

## 3. The evidence that moved it






**The vaccine thread's best clinical evidence is from February 2024.**
[38246194](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38246194/) (*Lancet*) is KEYNOTE-942: individualised neoantigen therapy
mRNA-4157 plus pembrolizumab versus pembrolizumab alone in resected melanoma,
randomised. Nothing later in this corpus supports the neoantigen thread as
strongly, and by 2026-07 the same thread is being attacked on both its target
space and its selection method. The high-water mark is at the start.

**The regulator states its own case in NEJM, and the field answers that the risk
is small.** [38265704](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38265704/) is a perspective by Verdun and Marks of CBER on
secondary cancers after CAR-T: the FDA's own account of the action it has taken,
in the flagship clinical journal, over the names of the two officials running the
review. [38206604](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38206604/) carries the safety notice in *JAMA*. Against them
[38195751](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38195751/) (*Nat Med*) reviews the reports of T cell malignancies and
concludes that existing follow-up data suggest a low risk compared with other
cancer treatments — a reassurance, not a warning, and the safety signal that
would have constrained the platform is on this reading not borne out.

!!! note "Corrected 2026-08-27"
    This paragraph was headed "CAR-T's secondary-malignancy problem reaches NEJM
    in one month" and argued that "January's regulatory signal becomes February's
    flagship clinical literature — a four-week lag, which is the fastest this
    corpus records for anything". Both halves fail. [38265704](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38265704/) has no
    abstract because it is not a study: it is a three-page perspective, pages
    584-586, by two FDA officials, so the February item is the same regulatory
    action as December's and January's, not the literature responding to it.
    There is no lag between them because there are not two things. And
    [38195751](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38195751/) was carded as a refutation on the strength of "unanswered
    questions" in its title; its one-sentence abstract reaches the opposite
    conclusion, and its stance is now `supports`. A safety-reassurance commentary
    is in any case a weak fit for a thread whose claim is about the platform
    generalising beyond CD19; a later reader should feel free to drop it rather
    than inherit it.

**And the indication that saves the platform is already in NEJM.**
[38381673](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38381673/): CD19 CAR-T in autoimmune disease, a case series with follow-up.
The corpus's November 2025 briefing calls autoimmunity CAR-T's growth edge and
treats it as a recent turn. It is in the flagship clinical journal in February
2024.

**ctDNA is measured well and acted on nowhere.** [37972346](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37972346/) prospectively
validates HPV ctDNA after chemoradiation in cervical cancer: across 70 patients,
persistent ctDNA is independently associated with inferior two-year
progression-free survival — 82% against 24% for those still positive at three
months — with a median lead time to recurrence of 5.9 months. [37992871](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37992871/) pairs
ctDNA detectability with CT-derived tumour volume in 85 resected NSCLC patients
and a 32-patient validation cohort, and stratifies relapse risk. Both are clean
prognostic associations; neither is a treatment decision, and the first says so
in its own conclusion, which offers the assay to *future* intensification trials.
`ctdna-mrd` claims the analyte guides treatment and does not merely forecast it,
and all three of this month's ctDNA cards are `neutral`.

    reporting on.

## 4. Refutations

### (a) Landing on a tracked thread

The FDA perspective above is the month's refutation on `cell-therapy` and is
filed as one; the *Nature Medicine* commentary beside it is not, and now reads as
support. It is worth reading both against the same month's [38316518](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38316518/), a complete
response in gastric cancer from Claudin18.2 CAR-T — the target that in June 2026
becomes the first CAR-T approved anywhere for a solid tumour. Both the platform's
liability and its eventual solid-tumour success are visible in the same month.

### (b) Method credibility

[38200587](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38200587/) (*Bioinformatics*): pitfalls of machine learning models for
protein-protein interaction networks. The paper's finding is that the field had
no consistent evaluation framework, so its networks were not comparable and the
discrepancies between algorithms went unexplained; the benchmarking framework it
builds to fix that then shows algorithm design has little impact on performance
once functional-genomics features are in play. That is a credibility result about
how the models were being compared, and it replicates in human and yeast data.

!!! note "Corrected 2026-08-27"
    This entry read: "This is the direct ancestor of the July 2025 finding that
    sequence-based interaction predictors plateau at 0.65 — the same objection,
    seventeen months earlier, in the same journal." There is no plateau and no
    such number in the abstract. What it reports about sequence is the opposite
    shape: sequence-based and functional-genomics models are *complementary*, the
    first specialising in interactions involving hub proteins and the second
    doing better on lone ones. A later result was written backwards onto an
    earlier paper. The card has also lost `foundation-models`; these are classic
    supervised models, with nothing pretrained or general-purpose in the paper.

[38331411](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38331411/): *zero is not absence*. The standard handling of zeros in
microbiome differential-abundance testing is wrong and censoring-based analysis
is required. [38279041](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38279041/) (*Nat Genet*): adjusting for genetic confounders in
transcriptome-wide association studies improves discovery — which says the
unadjusted analyses already in the literature were confounded.
